blocks.md:
Some stems end in **ㅡ**, a vowel so weak it simply gets out of the way.

아프다 → 아프 + 아요 → **아파요**

The ㅡ vanishes, and the ending attaches to what is left.

blocks.h: Which ending, once ㅡ is gone?
blocks.md:
Look at the vowel **before** the ㅡ.

아프 → the vowel before ㅡ is **ㅏ** → 아요 → **아파요**
예쁘 → the vowel before ㅡ is **ㅖ** → 어요 → **예뻐요**

If there is no vowel before it at all, use **어요**: 쓰다 → **써요**.

**Every stem ending in ㅡ does this, there are no exceptions.** That makes it the friendliest pattern in Korean. Notice how much you can already say: 아파요, 바빠요, 배고파요 are three of the most common sentences in daily life.

items.tip: I have a headache. 아프다 → 아파요

blocks.q: 바쁘다 → ?  (the vowel before ㅡ is ㅏ)
blocks.why: ㅡ drops and ㅏ decides the ending → **바빠요**. 바뻐요 picks the wrong ending; 바쁘어요 and 바쁘아요 leave the ㅡ in place, which never happens.
ㅡ drops, and the ㅏ in 아 pulls **아요** → 아파요. The other three either keep the ㅡ or choose the wrong ending.

blocks.q: “I’m hungry.”  저 지금 ___  (배고프다)
blocks.why: ㅡ drops; the vowel before it is ㅗ, so 아요 → 배고파요.

blocks.meaning: I have a lot of work these days, so I’m really busy.
blocks.why: ㅡ drops and the ㅏ decides → **바빠요**. The others keep the ㅡ or take the wrong ending.

blocks.q: 예쁘다 → ?  (the vowel before ㅡ is ㅖ)
blocks.why: ㅖ is not ㅏ or ㅗ, so the ending is 어요 → **예뻐요**. 예빠요 picks 아요; the last two leave the ㅡ in place.

blocks.q: Match each verb with its 해요 form.
Write it yourself: **“My head hurts.”**  (head = 머리)
blocks.hint: The head is the thing doing the hurting, so it takes 이/가. And 아프다 loses its ㅡ.
blocks.why: 머리가 아파요. This is the sentence you will use at a pharmacy, worth having ready.

blocks.q: Say it out loud: “My head hurts.”

blocks.md:
A batch of adjectives end in **ㅂ**. Before a vowel ending, that ㅂ becomes **우**.

덥다 → 더 + **우** + 어요 → **더워요**

These are weather-and-taste words, which is exactly what beginners talk about.

**Not every ㅂ stem changes.** 입다 (to wear) and 좁다 (to be narrow) are regular: 입어요, 좁아요. There is no way to tell by looking, you learn which ones change as you meet them. The good news is that the irregular ones are mostly adjectives, and the common ones fit on the list above.

items.tip: This food is a bit spicy.

blocks.q: 춥다 → ?
blocks.why: ㅂ becomes 우, then 어요 attaches → **추워요**. 춥어요 and 춥아요 leave the ㅂ in place; 추어요 drops it without putting 우 there.
맵다 is one of the changing ones: ㅂ → 우 → **매워요**. The others keep the ㅂ or lose it without the 우.

blocks.q: One of these verbs does **not** change its ㅂ. Which?
blocks.why: 입다 is regular: 입어요. 덥다, 맵다 and 어렵다 all turn the ㅂ into 우: 더워요, 매워요, 어려워요.

blocks.q: “It’s cold today.”  오늘 ___  (춥다)

blocks.meaning: Korean is harder than I expected.
blocks.why: 어렵다 turns ㅂ into 우 → **어려워요**. 어렵어요 and 어렵아요 keep the ㅂ; 어려어요 drops it without the 우.

blocks.q: Match each adjective with its 해요 form.
Write it yourself: **“It’s so hot today.”**  (so = 너무)
blocks.hint: 오늘 is one of the time words that take no 에. And 덥다 turns its ㅂ into 우.
blocks.why: 오늘 너무 더워요. Adding 은 to 오늘 sets today apart from other days, both are natural.

blocks.q: Say it out loud: “It’s so hot today.”

title.en: Lesson 3. ㄷ Verbs That Turn into ㄹ

blocks.h: The ㄷ Irregular: ㄷ Changes to ㄹ
blocks.md:
When certain verbs ending in **ㄷ 받침** meet a suffix starting with a vowel (like **-아요 / -어요**), the **ㄷ** softens into **ㄹ**.

- **듣다** (to listen) → **들어요**
- **걷다** (to walk) → **걸어요**
- **묻다** (to ask) → **물어요**

Notice that this change only happens before **vowels**! Before consonants (like -고, -지만), the ㄷ stays:
- 듣고 (듣다 + 고)
- 걷지만 (걷다 + 지만)

items.tip: I listen to music with earphones. (듣다 → 들어요)
I walk in the park every morning. (걷다 → 걸어요)
I ask for directions I don’t know. (묻다 → 물어요)

blocks.q: How do you conjugate ‘듣다’ (to listen) with -어요?
blocks.why: 듣다 is a ㄷ-irregular verb. Before a vowel ending, ㄷ turns into ㄹ, and with -어요 it becomes **들어요**.

blocks.q: Match each ㄷ-irregular verb with its polite present form.

blocks.meaning: The weather is good, so I walk in the park with a friend.
blocks.why: 걷다 turns ㄷ into ㄹ before -어요 → **걸어요**.

blocks.q: 듣다 (to listen) / Complete the sentence: 「매일 한국어 라디오를 ___ .」
blocks.why: 듣다 changes ㄷ to ㄹ when attaching -어요, resulting in **들어요**.

blocks.q: Arrange the words to say: “I listen to music in my room.”

blocks.say: 매일 아침에 음악을 들으면서 공원을 걸어요.
blocks.rom: mae-il a-chim-e eum-ag-eul deul-eu-myeon-seo gong-won-eul geol-eo-yo
blocks.q: Read out loud: “Every morning I walk in the park while listening to music.”

title.en: Lesson 4. Sorting Regular from Irregular Verbs

blocks.h: Regular vs. Irregular: Telling Them Apart
blocks.md:
Not every verb with **ㄷ** or **ㅂ** is irregular! Some common verbs follow regular rules:

- **Regular ㄷ:** 닫다 → **닫아요** (not 달아요), 받다 → **받아요** (not 발아요)
- **Regular ㅂ:** 입다 → **입어요** (not 이워요), 잡다 → **잡아요** (not 자워요)

Learning the handful of regular ones keeps you from over-applying the rule!
Common trap: **닫다** (to close) and **달다** (to be sweet). If you change 닫다 into *달아요, it sounds like you are saying the door is sweet! Keep 닫다 regular: **문을 닫아요**.

items.tip: Because wind is blowing, I close the window. (닫다 is regular → 닫아요)
I receive a birthday gift. (받다 is regular → 받아요)
I wear a warm coat. (입다 is regular → 입어요)

blocks.q: Which verb changes its final consonant when followed by -아요/-어요?
blocks.why: 듣다 is irregular (들어요). 닫다 (닫아요), 받다 (받아요), and 믿다 (믿어요) all keep their ㄷ.

blocks.q: Which verb does NOT turn ㅂ into 우?
blocks.why: 입다 is regular: it becomes **입어요**. 춥다 (추워요), 덥다 (더워요), and 맵다 (매워요) all change ㅂ into 우.

blocks.q: Match each verb to its correct polite form.

blocks.meaning: It’s cold, so I close the door tight.
blocks.why: 닫다 is regular. Stem vowel is ㅏ, so it takes -아요 → **닫아요**.

blocks.q: Conjugate 입다 (to wear) into polite present tense: 「따뜻한 옷을 ___ .」
blocks.why: 입다 is a regular verb. The stem vowel is ㅣ, so it simply takes -어요 → **입어요**.

blocks.say: 날씨가 추워서 따뜻한 옷을 입고 문을 닫아요.
blocks.rom: nal-ssi-ga chu-wo-seo tta-tteut-han os-eul ib-go mun-eul dad-a-yo
blocks.q: Read out loud contrasting the irregular 춥다 and regular 입다 and 닫다.
Arrange the words to say: “I receive a letter from my friend.”
